category.title: Dynamic Programming
category.description: 1D, 2D, 3D DP, knapsack, LCS, LIS, grid DP, and DP on trees/graphs.

algorithms.title: Fibonacci DP
algorithms.summary: The basic DP pattern where we store previously calculated Fibonacci values instead of calculating the same values repeatedly.
explanation: Fibonacci follows the rule: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2).
A normal recursive solution calculates the same values many times.
In DP, store every calculated Fibonacci value in an array.
Start with base cases fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1.
For every next position, calculate it using the previous two values.
Because only the previous two values are required, the O(N) array can be optimized to O(1) space.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Demonstrates how storing previous results avoids repeated recursive calculations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the current answer depends on a small number of previous states.
wAnswers.whereUsed: It is mainly a teaching pattern and is also useful as the foundation for more complex DP.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each Fibonacci value is calculated only once.

algorithms.title: Climbing Stairs DP
algorithms.summary: Counts the number of ways to reach the top when each move can take one or two steps.
explanation: To reach stair i, we can come from stair i-1 or stair i-2.
Therefore dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
The first stair has one way to reach it.
The second stair has two ways: 1+1 or 2.
Only the previous two values are needed, so we can use constant space.

traceSteps: Therefore there are 8 different ways to reach stair 5.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts the number of ways to reach a destination using allowed step sizes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a state can be reached from a small number of previous states.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Path counting and state transition problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every stair is processed once.

algorithms.title: House Robber DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the maximum money that can be collected when adjacent houses cannot both be selected.
explanation: At every house we have two choices: rob it or skip it.
If we rob the current house, we cannot rob the previous house.
If we skip it, we keep the best answer from the previous house.
Therefore dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + money[i]).
Only the previous two answers are required.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maximum sum when adjacent elements cannot be selected together.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When each position gives a choice between taking it and skipping it, with a restriction on neighboring choices.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Resource selection and scheduling problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each house is considered exactly once.

codeTemplates.code:
def rob(nums):
    prev2 = 0
    prev1 = 0

    for money in nums:
        current = max(prev1, prev2 + money)
        prev2 = prev1
        prev1 = current

    return prev1

algorithms.title: Maximum Subarray DP (Kadane's Algorithm)
algorithms.summary: Finds the contiguous subarray having the maximum possible sum.
explanation: At every element, decide whether to start a new subarray or continue the previous one.
If the previous sum is negative, it is better to start again from the current element.
Maintain currentSum and bestSum.
currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]).
bestSum stores the maximum value seen so far.

traceSteps: Kadane's algorithm finds this in one pass.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the problem asks for the best contiguous range based on sum.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Array optimization and maximum gain problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each element is processed once with constant extra space.

codeTemplates.code:
def max_subarray(nums):
    current = nums[0]
    best = nums[0]

    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i])
        best = max(best, current)

    return best

algorithms.title: Grid DP - Unique Paths
algorithms.summary: Counts the number of ways to reach the bottom-right cell of a grid when movement is allowed only right or down.
explanation: Every cell can be reached from the cell above or the cell on the left.
Therefore dp[row][col] = dp[row-1][col] + dp[row][col-1].
The first row has only one way because we can only move right.
The first column also has only one way because we can only move down.
A one-dimensional DP array can reduce space from O(M*N) to O(N).

traceSteps: Each cell stores the number of ways to reach it.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts paths through a grid.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When movement between grid cells follows fixed directions.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Grid navigation and path-counting problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every grid cell is calculated once.

algorithms.title: Minimum Path Sum DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum cost required to travel from the top-left to the bottom-right of a weighted grid.
explanation: For every cell, we can arrive either from the top or from the left.
Take the smaller of those two previous costs.
Add the current cell's value.
Therefore dp[col] = grid[row][col] + min(dp[col], dp[col-1]).
The one-dimensional array stores the best cost for the current row.

traceSteps: DP compares all possible ways to reach each cell.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the cheapest path through a weighted grid.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When every grid cell has a cost and movement directions are fixed.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Path planning and optimization problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The cheapest path to a cell depends only on the cheapest paths to its predecessors.

algorithms.title: Coin Change DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum number of coins required to make a target amount.
explanation: Let dp[x] be the minimum number of coins needed to make amount x.
For every coin, if the coin can be used, update dp[x].
The transition is dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x-coin] + 1).
Initialize dp[0] = 0 because zero coins are needed to make amount zero.
If an amount cannot be created, return -1.

traceSteps: DP checks smaller amounts first and uses their answers to build the answer for 11.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the minimum number of items needed to reach a target sum.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When unlimited use of choices is allowed and the goal is minimum count/cost.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Currency systems, resource allocation, and optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every amount is solved once using already solved smaller amounts.

algorithms.title: Coin Change II - Counting Combinations
algorithms.summary: Counts the number of different combinations that can create a target amount using unlimited coins.
explanation: dp[amount] stores the number of combinations that create that amount.
Set dp[0] = 1 because there is one way to create zero: choose nothing.
Process coins in the outer loop so different orders of the same combination are not counted separately.
For every coin, update amounts from coin to target.
The transition is dp[value] += dp[value - coin].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts combinations that form a target sum.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When items can be reused and the order of selected items does not matter.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Counting ways to make amounts and resource combinations.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each coin and amount pair is processed once.

algorithms.title: 0/1 Knapsack DP
algorithms.summary: Maximizes total value when every item can be selected at most once and the total weight cannot exceed a capacity.
explanation: For every item, we have two choices: take it or skip it.
If we skip it, the answer stays dp[w].
If we take it, we gain its value and use the answer for remaining capacity.
The transition is dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-weight] + value).
Iterate capacity backwards so an item cannot accidentally be used more than once.

traceSteps: Choose item with weight 3 and value 4.
Choose item with weight 4 and value 5.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maximizes value under a capacity constraint.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When every item can be selected zero or one time.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Resource allocation, budget selection, and subset optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each item is processed once and every capacity stores the best value possible.

algorithms.title: Unbounded Knapsack DP
algorithms.summary: Maximizes value when every item can be selected any number of times.
explanation: Unlike 0/1 Knapsack, an item can be selected again.
For every capacity, try every item that fits.
If we take an item, we can still use the same item again.
Therefore capacity is processed from small to large.
The transition is dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-weight] + value).

traceSteps: Take the item with weight 2 multiple times.
Take the item with weight 3 when useful.
DP checks repeated use of each item.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maximizes value when items can be used unlimited times.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the same choice can be selected repeatedly.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Rod cutting, coin systems, and unlimited resource selection.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each capacity uses the best answer for a smaller capacity.

algorithms.title: Subset Sum DP
algorithms.summary: Determines whether a subset of numbers can produce a target sum.
explanation: dp[s] tells whether sum s can be created using the processed numbers.
Initially only sum 0 is possible.
For every number, either use it or skip it.
Process sums backwards so the same number is not used more than once.
This is one of the most important forms of 0/1 Knapsack.

traceSteps: Therefore a subset with sum 11 exists.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether a target sum can be created from a subset.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When every number can be selected at most once.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Partition, target sum, and subset optimization problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each sum is updated using each number only once.

algorithms.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
algorithms.summary: Determines whether an array can be divided into two subsets having the same sum.
explanation: First calculate the total sum.
If the total sum is odd, equal partition is impossible.
Otherwise each subset must have sum total/2.
Now the problem becomes a standard subset sum problem.
Use boolean DP to determine whether total/2 can be created.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether an array can be split into two equal-sum subsets.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the problem asks to divide numbers into equal or target sums.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Partition and balancing problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: It converts the problem into one subset-sum DP.

algorithms.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N²) DP / O(N log N) optimized
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest subsequence in which every next element is greater than the previous element.
explanation: dp[i] represents the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i.
For every earlier index j, if nums[j] < nums[i], nums[i] can extend that subsequence.
The transition is dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).
The simple DP solution takes O(N²).
A faster O(N log N) solution uses binary search and a tails array.

traceSteps: The O(N²) DP checks all previous elements for each current element.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When elements must be selected in order but do not need to be contiguous.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Sequence analysis, scheduling, and optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each position stores the best subsequence ending there.

algorithms.title: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest sequence that appears in both strings while keeping the relative order of characters.
explanation: dp[i][j] represents the LCS length between the first i characters of string A and first j characters of string B.
If the current characters are equal, they can be included in the subsequence.
Then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
If they are different, skip one character from either string.
Then dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

traceSteps: Characters remain in the same relative order.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest ordered sequence common to two strings.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When comparing sequences while allowing characters to be skipped.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Diff tools, version comparison, DNA sequence analysis, and text comparison.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every pair of prefixes is solved once.

algorithms.title: Longest Common Substring DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest contiguous substring that appears in both strings.
explanation: Unlike LCS, the matching characters must be next to each other.
dp[i][j] stores the length of the common substring ending at A[i-1] and B[j-1].
If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
If they do not match, dp[i][j] becomes zero because the substring is broken.
Track the maximum value seen.

traceSteps: Therefore the longest common substring has length 4.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest contiguous sequence common to two strings.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When matching characters must be consecutive.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Document comparison and sequence analysis.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every pair of character positions is processed once.

algorithms.title: Edit Distance DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to transform one string into another.
explanation: dp[i][j] represents the minimum operations needed to convert the first i characters of A into the first j characters of B.
If the current characters are equal, no operation is needed.
Otherwise we can insert, delete, or replace a character.
Take the minimum of those three choices and add one.
The base cases are converting an empty string into another string using insertions or deletions.

traceSteps: Convert 'horse' to 'rorse' by replacing h with r.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Measures how many edits are needed to transform one string into another.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When insertion, deletion, and replacement operations are allowed.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Spell checkers, autocomplete, fuzzy search, and text comparison.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each pair of string prefixes is solved once.

algorithms.title: Word Break DP
algorithms.summary: Determines whether a string can be split into valid dictionary words.
explanation: dp[i] means the prefix ending before index i can be formed using dictionary words.
Start with dp[0] = true because an empty prefix is valid.
For every ending position, try possible starting positions.
If the previous prefix is valid and the substring exists in the dictionary, mark the current position as valid.
This converts a recursive word splitting problem into DP.

traceSteps: The prefix 'leet' exists in the dictionary.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether a string can be segmented into dictionary words.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a string must be divided into valid pieces.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Autocomplete, text segmentation, tokenization, and word processing.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each prefix is checked using previously solved prefixes.

algorithms.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest subsequence that reads the same forward and backward.
explanation: dp[left][right] represents the longest palindromic subsequence inside that range.
If the two boundary characters are equal, they can be included together.
Otherwise skip either the left character or the right character.
The transition is max(dp[left+1][right], dp[left][right-1]) when the boundary characters differ.
Build the table from shorter ranges to longer ranges.

traceSteps: DP checks smaller intervals and builds larger intervals.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest palindromic subsequence.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When characters can be skipped but their original order must remain.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Sequence analysis and palindrome optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every substring range is solved once.

algorithms.title: Palindrome Partitioning DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum number of cuts needed to divide a string into palindromic pieces.
explanation: First determine whether every substring is a palindrome.
Then dp[i] represents the minimum cuts needed for the prefix ending at i.
Try every previous position as the start of the last palindrome.
If that substring is a palindrome, update the minimum number of cuts.
This separates palindrome checking from minimum partition calculation.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the minimum cuts needed to partition a string into palindromes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a string must be split into valid palindromic sections.
wAnswers.whereUsed: String segmentation and palindrome problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every possible substring is checked once.

algorithms.title: Matrix Chain Multiplication DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to multiply a chain of matrices.
explanation: Matrix multiplication order affects the total number of operations.
dp[i][j] stores the minimum cost to multiply matrices from i to j.
Try every possible position k as the final split.
The cost is the left cost plus right cost plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices.
Choose the split with the smallest cost.

traceSteps: The better order gives a cost of 18000 scalar multiplications.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the cheapest way to parenthesize a sequence of matrix multiplications.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the problem asks for the best way to split an interval into smaller intervals.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Matrix computation and interval optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every interval is solved by checking all possible split points.

algorithms.title: Burst Balloons Interval DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the maximum coins that can be collected by bursting balloons in the best possible order.
explanation: The difficult part is that bursting a balloon changes its neighbors.
Instead of choosing the first balloon, choose the last balloon burst inside an interval.
When a balloon is the last one, its left and right neighbors are fixed.
dp[left][right] stores the best result for an interval.
Try every possible last balloon and take the maximum.

traceSteps: Add virtual balloons with value 1 at both ends.
Try every balloon as the last balloon in an interval.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Optimizes the order of operations where each operation changes neighboring elements.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When choosing the first operation makes the remaining problem difficult, but choosing the last operation makes the interval independent.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Classic interval DP problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every interval considers every possible final operation.

algorithms.title: Rod Cutting DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the maximum revenue obtained by cutting a rod into pieces with given prices.
explanation: dp[length] stores the maximum revenue possible for a rod of that length.
Try every possible first cut.
If the first piece has length cut, add its price to the best answer for the remaining length.
The transition is dp[length] = max(price[cut] + dp[length-cut]).
This is an unbounded knapsack-style DP because a piece length can be used repeatedly.

traceSteps: Cut the rod into two pieces of length 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maximizes revenue by choosing how to divide a rod.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a total length must be divided into reusable piece sizes.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Cutting and resource allocation optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every smaller rod length is solved before larger lengths.

algorithms.title: Stock Trading DP
algorithms.summary: Uses DP states to represent whether we currently hold a stock and how many transactions are available.
explanation: Stock problems are usually state-machine DP problems.
A state can represent whether we are holding a stock, not holding one, or have completed a certain number of transactions.
For each price, calculate the best answer for every possible state.
The next state depends on buying, selling, or doing nothing.
Different stock problems change the number of states and allowed transitions.

traceSteps: The DP state tracks the best result while holding or not holding the stock.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Optimizes profit under stock trading restrictions.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When buying, selling, cooldown, transaction limits, or transaction fees are involved.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Financial optimization and state-machine DP.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each day updates a small fixed number of states.

codeTemplates.code:
def max_profit(prices):
    cash = 0
    hold = float('-inf')

    for price in prices:
        cash = max(cash, hold + price)
        hold = max(hold, -price)

    return cash

algorithms.title: Tree DP - House Robber III
algorithms.summary: Uses DP on a tree where choosing a node prevents choosing its direct children.
explanation: For every tree node calculate two answers.
The first answer means we rob this node.
The second answer means we do not rob this node.
If we rob the current node, we cannot rob its children.
If we do not rob it, each child can either be robbed or skipped.

traceSteps: Do not rob its direct children.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Optimizes selections on a tree with parent-child restrictions.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the answer for a node depends on whether that node is selected.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Tree optimization and hierarchical decision problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each tree node is processed once.

algorithms.title: Dynamic Programming on DAG
algorithms.summary: Uses topological ordering to calculate DP values on a Directed Acyclic Graph.
explanation: A DAG has no directed cycle.
Because there are no cycles, nodes can be arranged in topological order.
Process nodes in that order so all required previous states are already calculated.
For each edge u → v, update the DP value of v using the value of u.
This can solve shortest path, longest path, and counting problems on DAGs.

exampleTrace.output: DP values calculated in topological order
traceSteps: Use node 0's value to update nodes 1 and 2.
Then use those values to update node 3.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Solves optimization or counting problems over directed acyclic graphs.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the state transitions form a DAG.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Dependency systems, project planning, and graph optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every vertex and edge is processed once.

practiceProblems.title: GeeksForGeeks - Shortest Path in Directed Acyclic Graph

algorithms.title: Bitmask DP
algorithms.summary: Uses bits to represent which elements have already been selected.
explanation: A bitmask is a binary number where each bit represents whether an element is selected.
For example, mask 0101 means elements 0 and 2 are selected.
dp[mask][i] can represent the best answer when the selected elements are mask and the current position is i.
Try adding every unused element to the current state.
This is useful when N is small, usually around 15 to 25 depending on the problem.

traceSteps: DP stores the best answer for each subset.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Solves subset-state problems where the number of elements is small.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the state depends on exactly which elements have already been selected.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Traveling Salesman, assignment problems, Hamiltonian paths, and subset optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: It avoids recomputing the same subset state.

practiceProblems.title: LeetCode 847 - Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes

algorithms.title: Digit DP
algorithms.summary: Counts numbers in a large range while satisfying conditions on their digits.
explanation: Digit DP builds a number one digit at a time.
The state usually contains the current digit position.
A tight flag tells whether the number is still equal to the upper bound prefix.
A started flag tells whether a real digit has been placed yet.
Additional state can store digit sum, remainder, previous digit, or used digits.

exampleTrace.input: Count numbers from 0 to 999 with digit sum 10
exampleTrace.output: The DP counts valid numbers digit by digit
traceSteps: Start from the most significant digit.
Use the tight flag to ensure the number does not exceed 999.
Reuse states when the same position and remaining state occur again.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts numbers satisfying digit-based restrictions over very large ranges.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When N is huge and the condition depends on its digits.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Number theory, digit restrictions, and competitive programming.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: It groups many numbers into the same digit state instead of processing every number.

algorithms.title: Tree DP
algorithms.summary: Solves optimization problems on trees by calculating answers for subtrees and combining child results.
explanation: Root the tree at any node.
Solve the problem for every child subtree first.
Combine child answers to calculate the answer for the current node.
The DP state can contain multiple values depending on whether the current node is selected or not.
Some advanced tree DP problems require rerooting to calculate the answer for every possible root.

exampleTrace.input: A tree where each node has a value
exampleTrace.output: Best answer calculated for the complete tree
traceSteps: Combine the values from all children.
The root's DP value gives the final answer.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Solves optimization and counting problems on trees.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a node's answer depends on answers from its children or subtree.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Hierarchical optimization, network problems, and tree algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each subtree is solved once instead of repeatedly.

practiceProblems.title: LeetCode 124 - Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum

algorithms.title: Rerooting DP
algorithms.summary: Calculates a DP answer for every possible tree root by reusing information from a previously processed root.
explanation: First root the tree at an arbitrary node and calculate subtree answers.
Then perform a second traversal.
When moving the root from u to its child v, reuse the answer already calculated for u.
Remove v's contribution from u and add u's contribution to v.
This allows answers for all possible roots to be calculated in linear time.

exampleTrace.output: Answer calculated for every possible root
traceSteps: First calculate subtree information with root 0.
Then move the root from 0 to 1.
Continue moving the root through the tree.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds a tree DP answer for every possible root efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the same tree problem must be solved with every node considered as the root.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Sum of distances, tree eccentricity, subtree contribution, and tree optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: A second traversal reuses previous results instead of solving the whole tree repeatedly.

practiceProblems.title: LeetCode 834 - Sum of Distances in Tree

algorithms.title: Interval DP
algorithms.summary: Solves problems where the state represents an interval [L,R] and the answer is built by splitting that interval.
explanation: dp[L][R] represents the best answer for the interval from L to R.
Try every possible split point or final operation inside the interval.
Combine the answers of the left and right intervals.
Process shorter intervals before longer intervals.
Matrix Chain Multiplication and Burst Balloons are classic examples.

exampleTrace.output: Best value for the complete interval
traceSteps: For every interval, try all possible split positions.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Optimizes operations performed on ranges or intervals.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the problem naturally asks for the best result inside a range.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Matrix multiplication, partitioning, merging, and game problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every interval is solved once and every possible split is considered.

practiceProblems.title: LeetCode 1039 - Minimum Score Triangulation of Polygon

algorithms.title: Game Theory DP / Minimax DP
algorithms.summary: Uses DP to determine the best result for a player when two or more players make optimal decisions.
explanation: Assume every player makes the best possible move.
dp[state] represents the best advantage or result from that state.
A player chooses the move that gives the best result for themselves.
The opponent's best response is included in the transition.
Many two-player problems can use a min/max recurrence.

traceSteps: The first player chooses an element from one end.
The second player then chooses optimally.
DP calculates the best score difference for every interval.
The initial interval determines whether the first player can win.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the best result when multiple players make optimal choices.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When players alternate turns and the future depends on previous choices.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Competitive games, optimal strategy, and adversarial decision problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The DP stores the best possible result from every game state.

algorithms.title: Probability DP
algorithms.summary: Calculates probabilities or expected outcomes by storing probability values for previously solved states.
explanation: A state represents the current situation of the random process.
Each possible next action has a probability.
The probability of reaching a state is calculated from previous states.
For expected value problems, multiply each outcome by its probability and add them.
The important part is identifying the state and all possible transitions.

exampleTrace.input: Probability of reaching a target after several random moves
exampleTrace.output: Probability stored in the final state
traceSteps: Start with probability 1 at the initial state.
Distribute probability according to possible moves.
Combine probabilities that reach the same state.
The final state contains the required probability.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes probabilities or expected values over repeated states.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a random process has overlapping states.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Random walks, probability games, and expected-value problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The same probability state is calculated only once.

algorithms.title: Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) DP
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum-cost tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the starting city using bitmask DP.
explanation: The important state is which cities have already been visited.
Represent visited cities using a bitmask.
dp[mask][i] stores the minimum cost when the visited cities are mask and the current city is i.
Try every city that has not been visited yet.
Finally add the cost of returning to the starting city.

traceSteps: Represent the visited set using a bitmask.
When all cities are visited, return to city 0.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the cheapest route visiting every city exactly once.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When N is small and the state depends on the exact set of visited nodes.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Routing, logistics, and combinatorial optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Bitmask DP merges identical visited-set states.

algorithms.title: Minimum Cost / Maximum Value State DP
algorithms.summary: A general DP pattern where each state stores the minimum cost or maximum value achievable up to that point.
explanation: Define dp[i] as the best answer when reaching position i.
For every allowed previous state j, calculate the new cost or value.
Take minimum for minimization problems or maximum for maximization problems.
The important step is identifying which previous states can transition into the current state.
This pattern appears in stairs, jumps, scheduling, partitioning, and many optimization problems.

traceSteps: For each position, look at all allowed previous positions.
The final position contains the answer.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: General minimum or maximum optimization problems.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a state can be reached through multiple previous states.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Scheduling, jumps, paths, and resource optimization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each state keeps only the best result needed by future states.

algorithms.title: Counting DP
algorithms.timeComplexity: Depends on number of states and transitions
algorithms.summary: Counts how many valid ways exist instead of finding a minimum or maximum value.
explanation: The DP state stores the number of valid ways to reach that state.
Start from a base state with one valid way.
For every transition, add the number of ways from the previous state.
Use modulo arithmetic when the answer can become very large.
The same idea appears in path counting, coin combinations, decoding, and string construction.

exampleTrace.input: Number of ways to reach stair 5 using jumps of 1 or 2

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts the number of valid solutions.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When the question asks 'how many ways' instead of best/minimum/maximum.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Combinatorics, path counting, decoding, and partition problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each state combines counts from previously calculated states.

algorithms.title: DP Space Optimization
algorithms.spaceComplexity: Reduced from O(N²) to O(N) where applicable
algorithms.summary: Reduces DP memory by keeping only the previous states required to calculate the next state.
explanation: Many DP tables contain old values that are no longer needed.
If the current row only depends on the previous row, keep only two rows.
If the current state only needs one previous row, one array can be enough.
For example, LCS can be optimized from O(N*M) space to O(M).
Space optimization does not change the time complexity.

exampleTrace.input: 2D DP where row i depends only on row i-1
traceSteps: Repeat until the final row is calculated.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Reduces the memory used by a DP solution.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When each state depends only on a small number of previous rows or states.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LCS, edit distance, grid DP, and knapsack.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Unnecessary old states are discarded.
